summary: Title slide introducing ERwait, a forecasting project for ER wait times, presented as an MScAC internship by Alex Chen.
questions: What is the main question this project answers for hospital operations?
Why is the hospital network described as fictional, and what data does this rely on?

summary: The slide motivates the project: ER waits are long and unpredictable, about 1 in 20 patients leave unseen, so the goal is a per-hospital 4-hour wait forecast.
claims: Emergency room waits are long and unpredictable
About 1 in 20 patients leave without being seen
The goal is to forecast the next 4 hours of wait time per hospital
weak_points: The '~1 in 20' figure has no source, time period or hospital scope, so the audience cannot check how large the problem is.
questions: Where does the 1 in 20 left-without-being-seen figure come from, and over what period?
How is 'long and unpredictable' measured, and what counts as a long wait?

summary: The slide asserts that the authors' model is 40% better than an unnamed baseline, shown by an unlabeled two-bar chart with no axes or values.
weak_points: The 40% figure has no stated baseline, metric, or test set, and the bar chart has no axis, labels, or values to verify it.
questions: Better than which baseline model, measured by what metric, on which held-out data?
What are the actual error values behind the 40% improvement, and is the difference statistically significant?

summary: The slide describes the dataset: two years of triage records with 1.2M visits, the features used, and an outlier-removal step.
claims: The dataset contains 2 years of triage records covering 1.2M visits.
Features include arrival time, triage level and time to first physician.
Outliers were removed from the data.
weak_points: Time to first physician is recorded after arrival and is closely tied to the wait being forecast, so using it as a feature risks target leakage.
Outlier removal is unexplained: no definition, threshold or count is given, and dropping extreme waits could remove the very long waits the model must predict.
questions: Is time to first physician known at the forecast time, or is it only recorded after the wait ends?
How did you define outliers, and how many of the 1.2M visits did removing them drop?

summary: The slide lists the modelling method: gradient-boosted trees implemented with LightGBM, validated with rolling-window validation.
claims: LightGBM was released by Google in 2020.
Rolling-window validation is used to evaluate the model.
weak_points: The LightGBM attribution is wrong: it was developed and released by Microsoft (open-sourced around 2016-2017), not by Google in 2020.
questions: Who developed LightGBM, and when was it first released?
What window sizes did rolling-window validation use, and how were test periods separated from training?
Why was gradient-boosted trees chosen over simpler baselines for this forecast?

summary: The slide lists the engineered features used to forecast emergency room wait times, spanning lagged waits, arrivals, calendar, weather, staffing and hospital-capacity signals.
claims: Lagged wait times at 1h, 2h, 4h, 24h and 168h are informative predictors of future waits.
Staffing levels and triage mix per hour are included as predictors of wait times.
Time to first physician is a feature available for forecasting.
weak_points: Sixteen lines of text at small size is too dense to present; the speaker should name the few features that matter most.
Time to first physician is measured during the visit and likely occurs after the wait being predicted, so it could leak the target.
Ambulance offload delays, admitted-no-bed counts and triage mix are only known at or after forecast time, so their availability at prediction time is unclear.
questions: Which three features contribute most to forecast accuracy, and by how much?
Is time to first physician known at the moment the forecast is made?
Are all features available in real time when the 4-hour forecast is issued?

summary: The slide claims the forecasting system is ready for deployment across all Ontario hospitals.
claims: The system is ready for deployment across all Ontario hospitals.
weak_points: Readiness across all Ontario hospitals is asserted with no evidence, such as multi-site validation, deployment trials, or integration testing, and the deck only describes a fictional Toronto hospital network.
Ontario has many hospitals with differing triage practices, staffing and data systems, so the claim generalises far beyond the single-network data used for training.
questions: What evidence shows the model works at hospitals other than the Toronto network used for training?
Does the 40% headline result hold outside the single Toronto network, and against what baseline?
What integration, privacy approval and data-feed work remains before any Ontario hospital could use it?

summary: The closing slide lists the 4-hour-ahead per-hospital wait forecasts as the contribution, calls the result strong, and proposes adding real-time bed data.
claims: The project delivers 4-hour-ahead wait forecasts per hospital.
weak_points: 'Strong headline result' is asserted without restating any metric, baseline, or the 40% figure from slide 3, so the conclusion is unsupported on this slide.
questions: What exactly is the headline metric, and what baseline is the 40% improvement measured against?
Why is real-time bed data the most important missing input for the next version?
